index.title: Unix and Linux command-line tools: short guides with examples | sqx docs
index.description: Short, practical guides to cat, head, tail, wc, grep, sed, awk, cut, tr, sort, uniq, xargs, tee, find, curl, jq and sqlite3, with common options, examples and how to combine each with sqx.
index.lead: sqx is built to sit in a Unix pipeline, next to tools you may already use. These short guides cover the options you will reach for most, with copy-paste examples and a note on how each one works together with sqx. Every page links to the full official manual.

categories.title: View and slice files
categories.summary: Look at data, take the start or end of it, and count it.

categories.title: Search and transform text
categories.summary: Find lines, pick columns and rewrite text as it streams past.

categories.title: Combine commands
categories.summary: Find files, fan out work and keep copies of a stream.

categories.title: Web, JSON and databases
categories.summary: Fetch from the web, reshape JSON and open SQLite files.

tools.name: cat
tools.headline: print and join files
tools.summary: Print files and join several into one stream.
tools.description: cat (short for concatenate) writes one or more files to standard output, one after another. It is the usual way to start a pipeline from a file, and the simplest way to glue files together.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Squeeze runs of blank lines into one
Show tabs, line ends and other invisible characters (GNU). On macOS use -vet
examples: Join files into a new one
with_sqx: Start a query from a file
Whatever cat prints becomes the stdin table.
cat users.csv | sqx "SELECT name, plan FROM stdin LIMIT 5"
Query many JSON Lines files as one table
JSON Lines files can be joined with cat safely, because every line is a complete record.
cat logs/*.jsonl | sqx "SELECT type, COUNT(*) FROM stdin GROUP BY type"
tips: To combine CSV files that each have a header row, see tail -n +2 on the tail page, or load each file with sqx -f.

tools.name: head
tools.headline: show the first lines
tools.summary: Show the first lines of a file or stream.
tools.description: head prints the beginning of a file, 10 lines by default. Use it to peek at a file's header and format before you write a query, or to take a quick sample of a huge file.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
examples: See the header row of a CSV
with_sqx: Try a query on a sample first
Test a slow or complex query on the first thousand lines of a big file, then run it on everything.
head -n 1000 big.csv | sqx "SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM stdin GROUP BY country"
Look at the first rows of a result
sqx -f events=events.jsonl -o csv "SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY amount DESC" | head -n 4
tips: In SQL, LIMIT does the same job inside the query: SELECT * FROM stdin LIMIT 10.

tools.name: tail
tools.headline: show the last lines
tools.summary: Show the last lines of a file, or skip the first ones.
tools.description: tail prints the end of a file, 10 lines by default. It can also start from a given line, which is handy for dropping a header row, and it can follow a log file as it grows.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Print everything from line N onwards. -n +2 skips a header row
Keep the file open and print new lines as they are written
with_sqx: Combine CSV files that each have a header
Keep the header from the first file only, then append the data rows of every file.
{ head -n 1 january.csv; tail -n +2 january.csv; tail -n +2 february.csv; } | sqx "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stdin"
Query only the most recent entries
tail -n 500 access.jsonl | sqx "SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM stdin GROUP BY status"
tips: tail -f never finishes, and sqx waits for the end of its input, so don't pipe tail -f into sqx. Take a fixed number of lines with -n instead.

tools.name: wc
tools.headline: count lines, words and bytes
tools.summary: Count lines, words, characters and bytes.
tools.description: wc (word count) reports how many lines, words and bytes are in its input. Most of the time you want wc -l, the number of lines.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Count characters (differs from bytes for non-ASCII text)
examples: Lines in many files, with a total
with_sqx: Count the rows a query returns
With -o raw there is no header, so every line is one row.
sqx -f users=users.csv -o raw "SELECT email FROM users WHERE plan = 'pro'" | wc -l
Or count inside SQL
COUNT(*) is exact and ignores the header row, which wc -l would include.
sqx -f users=users.csv "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE plan = 'pro'"

tools.name: grep
tools.headline: search text for patterns
tools.summary: Print the lines that match a word or regular expression.
tools.description: grep reads its input line by line and prints every line that matches a pattern. It is the fastest way to find something in logs, source code or any text file, and to narrow a big file down before further processing.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Invert: print lines that do not match
Print only the number of matching lines
Search every file under a directory
Print only the names of files that match
Print only the matching part of each line
Use extended regular expressions (|, +, ? without backslashes)
examples: Find errors in a log, any case
Search a project with line numbers
with_sqx: Filter lines before loading
On a very large JSON Lines file, a quick grep shrinks the input before sqx parses it.
grep '"type":"purchase"' events.jsonl | sqx "SELECT ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue FROM stdin"
Or filter with REGEXP inside SQL
sqx supports REGEXP, so you can match patterns on a specific column instead of the whole line.
sqx -f logs=access_log.csv "SELECT ts, request_url FROM logs WHERE user_agent REGEXP '(?i)curl|python'"
Search query results
sqx -f users=users.csv -o csv "SELECT * FROM users" | grep -i acme
tips: Put patterns in single quotes so the shell doesn't interpret characters like *, $ or |.

tools.name: sed
tools.headline: find and replace in a stream
tools.summary: Edit text as it flows: replace, delete or print lines.
tools.description: sed (stream editor) applies editing commands to each line of its input. Its most common use is find and replace with s/old/new/, but it can also delete lines, print a range of lines, or edit files in place.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Replace the first match on each line
Replace every match on each line
Edit the file in place and keep a .bak backup (works on GNU and macOS)
examples: Edit a file in place with a backup
with_sqx: Clean a URL list before auditing it
Drop comments and blank lines, then check every URL.
sed -e '/^#/d' -e '/^$/d' urls.txt | sqx -i lines "SELECT url, http_status(url) AS status FROM stdin"
Use a semicolon-separated export
Some spreadsheet exports use ; between fields. Swap it for a comma when no field contains commas or semicolons.
sed 's/;/,/g' export.csv | sqx "SELECT * FROM stdin LIMIT 5"
tips: On macOS, sed -i needs a backup suffix argument: use -i.bak, or -i '' for no backup. GNU sed accepts plain -i.

tools.name: awk
tools.headline: process columns of text
tools.summary: A small language for splitting lines into fields and acting on them.
tools.description: awk splits each line into fields ($1, $2, …) and runs a short program on it. It is ideal for picking columns, filtering on a field value, and quick sums, especially on whitespace-separated output such as logs.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD (GNU awk is called gawk)
options: Field separator, for example -F, for commas or -F'\t' for tabs
Pass a variable into the program
Fields of the current line. $0 is the whole line, $NF the last field
Run code before the first line or after the last
examples: Sum a CSV column, skipping the header
with_sqx: Turn a web server log into a table
In the common log format, $1 is the client IP and $9 the status code. awk pulls them out; sqx groups and sorts.
awk '{print $1","$9}' access.log | sqx -no-header "SELECT c1 AS ip, COUNT(*) AS errors FROM stdin WHERE c2 >= 400 GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY errors DESC LIMIT 10"
tips: awk -F, does not understand quoted CSV fields such as "Rao, Asha". For real CSV files, load them with sqx, which parses quotes correctly.

tools.name: cut
tools.headline: pick columns from each line
tools.summary: Cut out selected fields or character ranges from each line.
tools.description: cut extracts columns from each line, either by delimiter-separated field number or by character position. It is simpler and faster than awk when all you need is a column or two.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Use the character C as the field delimiter (default: tab)
Fields to keep, such as 1,3 or 2-4
Character positions to keep, such as 1-10
with_sqx: Take a column from sqx output
TSV output works with cut's default tab delimiter.
sqx -f users=users.csv -o tsv -no-output-header "SELECT id, email FROM users" | cut -f2
Use sqx when the CSV has quoted fields
cut splits on every comma, even inside quotes. sqx parses CSV properly and selects columns by name.
sqx -f users=users.csv "SELECT name, email FROM users"

tools.name: tr
tools.headline: translate or delete characters
tools.summary: Replace, squeeze or delete individual characters.
tools.description: tr works on single characters rather than words: it maps one set of characters to another, deletes characters, or squeezes repeats. It reads only from standard input, so use it in a pipe or with <.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Map each character in the first set to the second
with_sqx: Turn a comma-separated list into rows
Each item becomes a line, and sqx -i lines makes each line a row.
echo "example.com,go.dev,iana.org" | tr ',' '\n' | sqx -i lines "SELECT line AS domain, dns_ip(line) AS ip FROM stdin"

tools.name: sort
tools.headline: order lines
tools.summary: Sort lines alphabetically, numerically or by a column.
tools.description: sort orders the lines of its input. By default it sorts as text; options switch to numeric or human-readable size order, reverse it, or sort on a particular field.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Keep only the first of identical lines
Use C as the field separator
Sort by field N, for example -k3,3n
examples: By the third CSV column, numerically
with_sqx: Remove duplicate URLs before fetching
Each duplicate would otherwise be one more row to process.
sort -u urls.txt | sqx -i lines "SELECT url, http_status(url) AS status FROM stdin"
Or sort inside SQL
ORDER BY understands numbers, dates and multiple columns, and keeps the header in place.
sqx -f sales=sales.csv "SELECT * FROM sales ORDER BY amount DESC, region"

tools.name: uniq
tools.headline: collapse and count duplicates
tools.summary: Merge repeated adjacent lines, optionally counting them.
tools.description: uniq removes or counts lines that repeat one after another. Because it only compares neighbouring lines, it is almost always used right after sort.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Prefix each line with how many times it occurred
Print only lines that are repeated
Print only lines that are not repeated
with_sqx: The SQL version of sort | uniq -c
The classic counting pipeline and the GROUP BY query give the same answer, but sqx skips the header and handles quoted CSV fields.

cut -d, -f4 users.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

cat users.csv | sqx "SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS n FROM stdin GROUP BY country ORDER BY n DESC"

tools.name: xargs
tools.headline: run a command for each input line
tools.summary: Turn lines of input into arguments for another command.
tools.description: xargs reads items from standard input and runs a command with those items as arguments. It connects tools that print lists (find, grep -l, sqx -o raw) to tools that take arguments, and can run several commands in parallel.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Use at most N items per command
Replace {} in the command with each item, running once per item
Run up to N commands at the same time
Items are separated by NUL characters (pair with find -print0)
Print each command before running it
examples: Delete files found by find, safely
Fetch headers for each URL, 4 at a time
with_sqx: Run a command for every result row
-o raw prints bare values, one per line, ready for xargs.
sqx -f users=users.csv -o raw "SELECT email FROM users WHERE plan = 'enterprise'" | xargs -n 1 echo notify:
Import every CSV file into one database
sqx import appends to the table and adds new columns when files differ.
find exports -name '*.csv' | xargs -I {} sqx import -db exports.db -t rows {}
tips: File names with spaces break plain xargs. Use find -print0 with xargs -0, or -I {} with one item per line.

tools.name: tee
tools.headline: save a stream and pass it on
tools.summary: Write input to a file and to the screen (or the next command) at once.
tools.description: tee copies its input to one or more files while also passing it through to standard output, like a T-shaped pipe fitting. Use it to keep a copy of intermediate results without breaking a pipeline.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Append to the file instead of overwriting it
with_sqx: Save a report while reading it
sqx -f users=users.csv -o md "SELECT plan, COUNT(*) AS users FROM users GROUP BY plan" | tee plans.md
Keep the raw prefetch results
Save what prefetch found, and keep a copy of it as a CSV file for later.
sqx prefetch -o csv < urls.txt | tee prefetch.csv | sqx "SELECT status_code, COUNT(*) FROM stdin GROUP BY status_code"

tools.name: find
tools.headline: locate files
tools.summary: Search a directory tree for files by name, type, age or size.
tools.description: find walks through directories and lists the files that match your tests: name, type, modification time, size and more. It can also run a command on each match.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Linux and BSD
options: Match the file name (use -iname to ignore case)
Don't descend more than N levels
Run a command on the matches
Separate results with NUL, for xargs -0
examples: All CSV files under the current folder
Logs changed in the last day
with_sqx: Query every JSON Lines file in a tree
find logs -name '*.jsonl' -exec cat {} + | sqx "SELECT type, COUNT(*) FROM stdin GROUP BY type"
tips: Quote patterns like '*.csv' so the shell passes them to find instead of expanding them itself.

tools.name: curl
tools.headline: transfer data from URLs
tools.summary: Download pages, call APIs and inspect HTTP responses.
tools.description: curl sends requests to URLs and prints the response. It supports every HTTP method, custom headers, authentication, file uploads and many other protocols, which makes it the standard tool for testing and scripting web APIs.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS, Windows 10+ and most Linux distributions
options: Fail with an error on HTTP 4xx and 5xx responses
Save the response to a file (-O uses the remote name)
Choose the method and send a request body
with_sqx: Query an API response
A JSON array of objects becomes a table with one row per object.
curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/golang/go/releases | sqx "SELECT tag_name, published_at FROM stdin LIMIT 5"
Or let sqx fetch and cache it
-f accepts a URL directly. The response is cached, so re-running the query doesn't hit the API again. Use curl when you need auth headers or POST.
sqx -f releases=https://api.github.com/repos/golang/go/releases "SELECT tag_name, published_at FROM releases LIMIT 5"

tools.name: jq
tools.headline: slice and reshape JSON
tools.summary: A command-line processor for filtering and transforming JSON.
tools.description: jq reads JSON and applies a filter to it: pick fields, walk into nested arrays, select matching items and build new objects. It pairs well with sqx: jq reshapes nested JSON into flat records, and sqx joins, groups and sorts them.
tools.availability: Install with brew install jq, apt install jq, dnf install jq or winget install jqlang.jq
options: Get a field, or a nested field
Keep items where the condition is true
Compact output, one JSON value per line (JSON Lines)
examples: Turn an array into JSON Lines
with_sqx: Unwrap nested records, then aggregate
Many APIs put the records inside a key such as items. jq pulls them out as flat JSON Lines; sqx does the grouping.

curl -s 'https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=sqlite+cli' \
  | jq -c '.items[] | {name: .full_name, stars: .stargazers_count, language}' \
  | sqx "SELECT language, COUNT(*) AS repos, SUM(stars) AS stars FROM stdin GROUP BY language ORDER BY stars DESC"
Or read nested fields in SQL
For one or two nested values, SQLite's json_extract is often enough.
sqx -f events=events.jsonl "SELECT id, json_extract(meta, '$.device') AS device FROM events"

tools.name: sqlite3
tools.headline: the SQLite command-line shell
tools.summary: Open, query and manage SQLite database files interactively.
tools.description: sqlite3 is the official interactive shell for SQLite databases. sqx writes ordinary SQLite files with import and -save, so you can open them in sqlite3 for interactive work, backups or schema changes.
tools.availability: Preinstalled on macOS and many Linux distributions; otherwise apt install sqlite3 or brew install sqlite
with_sqx: Build a database with sqx, explore it with sqlite3

sqx import -db project.db -t users users.csv
sqlite3 project.db "SELECT plan, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY plan"
tips: sqx's extra functions, such as http_status or html_title, exist only inside sqx. Run those queries with sqx -db project.db, and use sqlite3 for plain SQL.
